newsitem.title: BRAZIL: BRAZIL BLAMES CAPITAL GOODS FOR JULY TRADE GAP.
newsitem.headline: BRAZIL BLAMES CAPITAL GOODS FOR JULY TRADE GAP.

text.p: A surge in capital goods imports contributed to a wider-than-expected $811 million trade deficit in July, but the result does not herald any nasty trade surprises for the rest of the year, Brazilian officials said Monday.

Jose Roberto Mendonca de Barros, economic policy secretary at the Finance Ministry, told reporters the spike in capital goods imports probably resulted from a leak of government plans to end tariff exemption for 3,700 items.
"Before the decree came out, someone talked about it and it's reasonable to assume there was some anticipation (of imports)," Mendonca de Barros said.
Apart from the capital goods, Mendonca de Barros was at a loss to explain why the trade deficit in July came in above market expectations of a $570 million gap.
"I would have to say, imports and exports were simply strong. That's it," he said. "The real surprise was how strong the imports were in the last days of the month."
Initially, officials began to blame state-owned Petrobras for a burst in oil imports.
But figures show that oil and lubricant imports in July of $485 million were actually 14.8 percent lower than the $569 million imported in July 1996.

Petrobras did import the bulk of its oil -- some $150 million -- on the last day of the month, causing a sharp and unexpected last-minute deterioration in a trade deficit that up till then had looked reasonable rosy.
Capital goods imports of $1.707 billion in July were 53.8 percent higher than in the same month a year ago.
Imports of primary goods also rose in July, reaching $2.754 billion, compared with $2.224 billion in July 1996.
Aircraft and parts imports amounted to $250 million in July.
Consumer goods purchases abroad rose 23.9 percent year-on-year to hit $1.103 billion last month.
But Mendonca de Barros said the July result did not alter his view that the trade balance was coming under control.
"The fact that July's trade deficit was higher than expected doesn't alter the outlook for greater calm on the trade front," he said.
July's $811 deficit brought the trade gap for the year so far to $5.516 billion, almost as much as the $5.539 billion deficit posted in the whole of 1996.
